paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Hudson took place in southwest Georgia in August 1881, when crowds sought to kill Hudson, a Black man accused of an axe murder in Terrell County, first at the jail in Albany and then at Dawson. At Dawson a crowd of 1,500 to 2,000 people took him to the court house intending to execute him, but local citizens persuaded it to let him be jailed. Hudson was later convicted and sentenced to hang, after a Chicago paper had reported that he had probably been lynched.

According to an Atlanta dispatch, Hudson went to the farm of an elderly white man, David Lee, near Dawson, lured him out with word that his fences were on fire, and killed him with an axe. He was accused of then killing Mrs. Lee and a Black servant girl, striking down a second servant, and taking $500 from the house. The surviving servant raised the alarm, and the Chicago Tribune's correspondent wrote that Hudson would be lynched if captured.

Sheriff Edwards of Dougherty County and Marshal Westbrook overtook Hudson on Bates' plantation in Lee County and took him to the jail at Albany. On the night of Aug. 19 a telegram from Albany reported him there and asked for troops to keep the crowd from lynching him. The Tribune's correspondent wrote that the Albany Guards refused Mayor Wilder's call, saying he lacked authority, and that the sheriff's appeal to the Governor went unanswered because the Governor was away.

Hudson was then sent by train to Dawson, and the Albany News reported that every station along the line was crowded with people trying to see him. At Dawson he was taken from the car by 1,500 or 2,000 people "of both colors," carried to the court house, thrown from the doorway to the ground, and set on a table to describe the killings. When he fainted, prominent citizens used the pause to appeal for "law and order," the crowd was calmed, and he was lodged in jail.

Two other men, Matt Gregor and a man named Green, were arrested as implicated in the murders. In early September the Weekly Clarion reported Hudson's confession and the expectation that he would be "burned at the stake." Instead a jury in Terrell Superior Court found him guilty, and he was sentenced to be hanged at Dawson on Oct. 14, 1881. No report of the execution appears in the coverage, and no one was reported charged over the crowd's actions.

Northern papers carried the Atlanta wire, which concentrated on the murders and mentioned the lynching threat in a closing line, under headlines such as "Bloody Work by a Black Fiend in Georgia" and "A Fiendish Butchery." The Chicago Tribune ran its correspondent's report as "Probably Lynched," stating that public sentiment favored "lynch law" and that no effort would be made to prosecute any lynchers. Digest columns in New Jersey and elsewhere reprinted the story in late August with only his capture, while the Cambria Freeman said he had surrendered "to escape lynching."
The fullest account of the crowd came from the Albany News as summarized by the Savannah Morning News, which called Hudson "the negro murderer" and credited Dawson's citizens with restoring order.

Accounts differ on the night of the murders, given as Tuesday or Thursday, on whether Lee died in the woods or the house, and on how many servants were killed. The Southern Standard alone placed the crime near "Dover" and called the dead servant white, while the Cambria Freeman's surrender version conflicts with the Tribune's and Albany News's reports of a capture in Lee County.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Hudson
bases: Crowds sought to lynch Frank Hudson while he was held at Albany (A2, A3) and, at Dawson, carried him from the train to the court house 'bent on his immediate execution' before citizens restored order (A6); he was not killed.

A crowd of 1,500-2,000 seized Hudson at Dawson intent on executing him for the Lee murders, but he was lodged in jail alive (A6, A5), later convicted and sentenced to hang (A13, A14); the Tribune's report that he had 'probably' been lynched was a guess later contradicted (A3, A6).
The Atlanta wire (A2), the Chicago Tribune's own correspondent (A3) and the Albany News as quoted by the Savannah Morning News (A5, A6) independently report crowds threatening to lynch Hudson.

accounts.gist: Hudson was in jail at Albany and a telegram asked for military aid to keep the crowd from lynching him.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Atlanta correspondent
accounts.gist: The Albany Guards refused to protect the jail, public sentiment favored lynch law, and Hudson had probably been lynched.

accounts.label: Albany News (via Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: On the train to Dawson crowds gathered at every station; at Dawson 1,500-2,000 people carried him to the court house to execute him until citizens' appeals restored order and he was jailed.

accounts.label: Cambria Freeman brief
accounts.gist: Hudson surrendered himself to escape lynching.

framing.detail: The Atlanta wire ran under headlines such as 'Bloody Work by a Black Fiend in Georgia' and 'Three People Murdered by a Negro'.
The Chicago Tribune's 'Probably Lynched' reported the Guards' refusal and that lynchers would face no prosecution, without condemning the mob, while calling the crime 'unprovoked'.
The Savannah Morning News, quoting the Albany News, called Hudson 'the negro murderer' and credited 'prominent citizens' with restoring 'law and order'.
The Weekly Clarion called the crime 'fiendish' and reported he might be 'burned at the stake' without comment.
